title: Database Types, CAP and Choosing a Store
summary: Quick revision notes on relational vs NoSQL store families, CAP, ACID vs BASE, replication and sharding, and how to pick a database for a workload.

chapters.title: Database Families and Mental Model
points: Relational: fixed schema, tables and rows, SQL joins, strong transactions (PostgreSQL, MySQL)
Document: JSON-like docs with flexible schema, nested data read in one fetch (MongoDB)
Key-value: get/put by key only, fastest and simplest, no queries on values (Redis, DynamoDB)
Wide-column: rows keyed by partition key with sparse column families, built for huge write volume (Cassandra, HBase)
Graph: nodes and edges as first-class data, fast multi-hop traversals (Neo4j)

chapters.title: CAP Theorem
points: Consistency: every read sees the latest write; Availability: every request gets a non-error response; Partition tolerance: system keeps working when the network splits
Partitions are unavoidable in distributed systems, so the real choice is C or A during a partition
CP system refuses or errors some requests to stay consistent (HBase, MongoDB with majority writes)
AP system answers with possibly stale data and reconciles later (Cassandra, DynamoDB default)
CAP 'C' is linearizability, not the ACID 'C' (constraints); without a partition you can have both

chapters.title: ACID vs BASE
points: ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (constraints hold), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes)
BASE: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency; replicas converge if writes stop
Eventual consistency means a read right after a write may return old data
Tunable consistency: quorum with R + W > N guarantees reading the latest write (N=3, R=2, W=2)
Use ACID for money, inventory and orders; BASE for feeds, counters, carts and analytics

chapters.title: Replication and Sharding
points: Replication copies the same data to many nodes for availability and read scaling; sharding splits different data across nodes for write and storage scaling
Leader-follower: writes go to the leader, followers serve reads and may lag (replication lag causes stale reads)
Multi-leader and leaderless replication accept writes on several nodes, so conflicts need resolution (last-write-wins, vector clocks)
Range sharding supports range scans but creates hotspots; hash sharding spreads load evenly but breaks range queries
Consistent hashing adds or removes nodes by moving only about 1/N of keys; a bad shard key (low cardinality, monotonic id) causes hot shards

chapters.title: Choosing a Database and Common Mistakes
points: Start from access patterns: what queries, read/write ratio, consistency need, data size and growth
Default to a relational database (PostgreSQL) unless a clear need rules it out; it also handles JSON columns
Typical fits: Redis for cache and sessions, MongoDB for catalogs and content, Cassandra for time-series and event logs, Neo4j for recommendations and fraud rings
Mistake: choosing NoSQL for scale you do not have, then needing joins and transactions later
Mistake: one database for everything; polyglot persistence uses a primary store plus a cache or search index synced from it

chapters.title: Database Choice Cheat Sheet
points: Family to use case: relational = transactions and joins, document = flexible entities, key-value = cache/lookup, wide-column = massive writes, graph = relationships
CAP: CP = consistent but may reject, AP = available but may be stale
ACID = correctness first; BASE = scale and availability first
Replication = availability and reads; sharding = capacity and writes; shard key decides everything
Decision order: access pattern, consistency need, scale, then pick; default PostgreSQL
